393.title: Thunder on Sinai (Exodus 19)
393.hook: smoke, trumpet, trembling mountain, and a people at the foot
393.howItsDone: Christians read Exodus 19 as the prelude to the Ten Commandments, and some churches read it at Pentecost, whose story in Acts takes place on the Jewish feast of Shavuot, remembered in Jewish tradition as the time the law was given at Sinai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jethro watched Moses judge from sunrise to sunset and told him the truth. Your line was you can't do it alone. What did you hand over? Day three hundred ninety-three.

In the third month out of Egypt, the people come to a mountain in the desert and pitch their tents at its foot. They've seen a sea open. They've eaten bread that fell with the dew. And now Moses goes up and comes down, up and down, carrying messages. Wash your clothes, he tells them. Get ready. In three days something is going to happen. Put a boundary around the mountain, and don't touch it. On the morning of the third day, it starts. Thunder. Lightning. A cloud sitting heavy on the peak. And then a sound you wouldn't expect from a mountain: a trumpet, getting louder and louder. The whole camp trembles.
screen: `THE THIRD MONTH OUT OF EGYPT.` → `WASH, AND WAIT THREE DAYS.` → `A TRUMPET FROM THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible tells it like this: "there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled." Then the mountain itself: "mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire," and "the whole mount quaked greatly." Smoke like a furnace. A trumpet with no trumpeter. Notice what this scene is for. It isn't a lecture. Before a single law is given, the people are made to feel how big the One speaking is. Awe comes first. But it isn't only terror. Just before the thunder, God sends Moses down with a gentle message, remembering "how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself." And then a promise: you'll be a kingdom of priests, a holy nation. A whole people, not just a few, set apart. So the mountain shakes, but the voice has already said why they're here: unto myself. Where is Sinai? Honestly, nobody knows for sure. Christian tradition points to a peak in the south of the Sinai Peninsula, with an old monastery at its foot. Others have proposed other mountains. The Bible sometimes calls it Horeb, and it never pins it to a map. For Christians, this mountain echoes forward. Jewish tradition remembers the giving of the law at the feast of Shavuot. In Greek that feast is called Pentecost, and in the book of Acts, on the day of Pentecost, the Spirit comes with wind and fire.
screen: `THUNDER, CLOUD, TRUMPET, SMOKE.` · `AWE COMES BEFORE THE LAW.` · `ON EAGLES' WINGS, TO MYSELF.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHERE IT IS.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE MOUNT QUAKED GREATLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel awe at something vast. Settle, and breathe. Picture the biggest thing you've ever stood near. A mountain range. The ocean at night. A thunderstorm rolling in. A sky so full of stars it made you dizzy. Put yourself back at its foot. Notice how small you were next to it. Some people find that kind of smallness a relief, like being the right size. Stay there. If you pray, you can simply stand before God in that smallness, without words. If you don't, let the vastness be enough. The bell holds the time.
Sinai. The mountain in the desert where the people camped in the third month after Egypt, wrapped in smoke and thunder, where the law was given.
Your line: the mountain shook. Today, when you see something bigger than you, a storm, a skyline, a tree, stop for five seconds and let it be big. Day three hundred ninety-three.

394.title: The ten words, part one (Exodus 20:1–11)
394.hook: no other gods, no idols, God's name in honor, the sabbath kept
394.howItsDone: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism classes and Sunday schools, and some churches read them aloud in worship; Catholic and Lutheran catechisms number them one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sinai: thunder, smoke, a trumpet growing louder, and a people trembling at the foot. Your line was the mountain shook. What did you see today that was bigger than you? Day three hundred ninety-four.

They hang on courthouse walls and in Sunday school classrooms. They've been carved in stone, stitched on samplers, fought over in lawsuits, and turned into a movie with a parting sea. Can you name all ten? And which one comes first? No other gods is a fair guess. But that isn't quite the first thing the voice on the mountain says. Before a single command, there's a sentence about who is speaking, and what he has already done. Today, the first half of the ten words: the ones about God.
screen: `ON WALLS, IN STONE, IN COURT.` → `CAN YOU NAME ALL TEN?` → `WHAT COMES FIRST?`

segments.voice: Here is how the voice begins, in the King James Bible: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." A rescue comes before any rule. You're already free, the text says, and here is how free people live. Then: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." No carved image to bow down to. Don't take God's name in vain, which means more than swearing: don't use the name emptily, or to prop up a lie. And then: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Six days of work, and a seventh day of rest, for you, your children, your servants, the stranger living with you, even your cattle. The reason given is creation: God rested on the seventh day. In Hebrew, Exodus calls them aseret ha-devarim, the ten words. Decalogue is the Greek version of that phrase: deka, ten, logos, word. And traditions count the ten differently. In Jewish tradition, the opening sentence, I am the LORD thy God, is the first word. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, put no other gods and no images together, and split coveting into two at the end. Orthodox Christians and Reformed and Anglican churches make the images a separate second commandment. Same text, different ways of numbering it, and nobody is leaving anything out. What all of them see is the order. The first words point at God. Everything else follows from what you put first.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you put first. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last week. What got your first hour in the morning? What did you check before anything else? What do you rearrange everything else around? Don't judge the answer. Just name it, honestly. Then ask a second question: is that what I'd choose to put first, if I were choosing? If you pray, you can hear the opening line again: I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out. If you don't, simply hold the question. The bell holds the time.
Decalogue. Greek for the ten words, the Bible's own name for the commandments given at Sinai. The first ones are about God.
Your line: first things first. Tomorrow morning, before the phone, give the first minute to whatever you most want to come first. Day three hundred ninety-four.

what a scholar hears: aseret ha-devarim, the ten words, numbered one way in Jewish tradition, another by Catholics and Lutherans, another by Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches.

395.title: The ten words, part two (Exodus 20:12–17)
395.hook: honor parents, no murder, adultery, stealing, lying or coveting
395.tomorrow: The stranger, the widow, the orphan
395.howItsDone: Many Christians use the Ten Commandments to examine their conscience, especially before confession or communion, and churches teach them in catechism classes as the shape of love for God and neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first half of the Decalogue: a rescue, then no other gods, no images, no empty use of the name, and a day of rest. Your line was first things first. What got your first minute? Day three hundred ninety-five.

Picture an ordinary street. A teenager rolling her eyes at her dad. A man at a bar, angry enough to swing. A couple drifting toward an affair over text. A cashier slipping a twenty into his pocket. Someone giving a statement to the police that bends the truth. And a neighbor staring over the fence at a nicer car, a bigger house, a happier-looking marriage, and feeling something sour rise. Six scenes. Every one of them is covered by the second half of the ten words. The first half turned toward God. Now the voice on the mountain turns to the people next door.
screen: `SIX SCENES ON ONE STREET.` → `THE FIRST HALF FACED GOD.` → `NOW, THE PEOPLE NEXT DOOR.`

segments.voice: It starts at home, in the King James Bible: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." Centuries later, in his letter to the Ephesians, Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise. Then come three commands so short they're almost blunt. "Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal." In Hebrew each of those is just two words. Lo tirtzach. Lo tinaf. Lo tignov. You could carve them on a tablet without running out of room. One detail many people ask about: the verb in lo tirtzach is usually used for unlawful killing, which is why many modern translations say murder. The law elsewhere still deals with war and capital cases, so readers have argued over its edges for centuries. Then, no false witness against your neighbor: in a world with no cameras, a lie in court could cost someone their life. And then the last one, and it's different from all the rest. Thou shalt not covet: your neighbor's house, spouse, servants, ox, donkey, anything that is your neighbor's. Every other command is about something you do. This one is about something you want. It reaches inside. You could keep the other nine perfectly and still break the tenth in your own kitchen, staring out the window. Christians often hear the two halves as two tables: love of God, and love of neighbor. Jesus, asked for the greatest commandment, gave an answer with exactly that shape. We'll come back to it in a couple of weeks.
screen: `HONOR PARENTS: A COMMAND WITH A PROMISE.` · `THREE COMMANDS, TWO WORDS EACH.` · `NO FALSE WITNESS.` · `THE LAST ONE IS ABOUT WANTING.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT NOT COVET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one of the six, and keep it carefully today. Settle, and breathe. Walk slowly down the list in your mind. Honor parents. No killing. No adultery. No stealing. No false witness. No coveting. One of them will catch, a little. Maybe it's the parent you haven't called. Maybe it's the small exaggeration you tell about a coworker. Maybe it's the scrolling that leaves you wanting someone else's life. Pick that one. Picture keeping it, on purpose, just for today. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Lo tirtzach. Hebrew for thou shalt not kill, from a verb usually meaning unlawful killing, one of the ten words carved for neighbor and self.
Your line: ten words for living. Today, keep the one you chose, carefully, from now until you sleep, and notice how often it comes up. Day three hundred ninety-five.

396.title: The stranger, the widow, the orphan (Exodus 22:21–27)
396.hook: you were strangers in Egypt; if he cries to me, I will hear
396.howItsDone: Some churches run food pantries, refugee resettlement programs and ministries to widows and orphans, and some Christians cite Exodus 22 and Matthew 25 together when explaining why.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of the ten words, lo tirtzach among them, ending with the one about wanting. Your line was ten words for living. Which one did you keep carefully? Day three hundred ninety-six.

It's your first week in a new country. You don't know which line to stand in. You can't read the forms. Someone at a counter speaks to you slowly and loudly, as if you were a child, and the people behind you sigh. You smile, because you need what's at the end of that line. A new school, a new job, a hospital in another city can give a small taste of it. Right after the ten words, Exodus starts filling in what they look like on the ground. And soon the law turns to exactly that person: the one who doesn't belong yet.
screen: `YOUR FIRST WEEK IN A NEW COUNTRY.` → `THE WRONG LINE, THE WRONG FORM.` → `THE LAW TURNS TO THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger: someone living among a people who isn't one of them. Not a tourist. A neighbor without roots, without land, without family to stand up for him. And notice the reason. Not, because it's polite. Because you remember. You were the ones in the wrong line once. A chapter later the law says it again even more tenderly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Then the circle widens. "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." In the world of the text, a widow or an orphan could easily be left with no one to speak for them, and nothing to stop them being pushed aside. And here the text does something startling. God steps in personally. If you afflict them and they cry to me, he says, I will surely hear their cry. Then the law gets very small and very practical. If you lend to a poor neighbor, don't charge interest. If you take his cloak as a pledge, give it back before the sun goes down. Why? Because "that is his covering only," and the text asks, wherein shall he sleep? And God's reason: "when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious." Some Christians hear an echo in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The stranger, the widow, the orphan: three people with no one else to stand up for them.
screen: `GER: SOMEONE WITHOUT ROOTS.` · `YOU KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THE WIDOW AND THE ORPHAN.` · `GIVE BACK THE CLOAK BY SUNDOWN.` · then, large: `FOR YE WERE STRANGERS IN THE LAND OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to someone in need. Settle, and breathe. First remember a time you were the stranger: new, lost, unsure where to stand. Feel it again for a moment. Then think of someone who's there now. A new coworker. A family who just moved in. A person on the corner you pass every day. Someone grieving, or a kid without much of a home. Pick one person, and one small thing you could give: food, money, time, a name remembered. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The stranger. In Hebrew, ger: someone living among you without land or family. The law protects him because Israel remembers being one.
Your line: you were strangers too. Today, give one real thing to someone who's new, alone or in need, and give it before the sun goes down. Day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: The golden calf (Exodus 32)
397.hook: Moses is late, so they melt their earrings into a god they can see
397.howItsDone: Some Christian preachers use the golden calf to talk about modern idols such as money, success or control, and some churches read the story alongside the giving of the law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stranger, the widow and the orphan, and a cloak handed back before sundown. Your line was you were strangers too. Who did you give to? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Moses has gone up the mountain. A day passes. A week. The cloud sits on the peak and nothing comes down. Two weeks. Three. Forty days, the text says, and forty nights. Down in the camp, people start to talk. Where is he? Is he dead up there? Who's in charge now? And then a crowd gathers around Aaron, Moses' brother, the one left behind to lead. And they say, in the King James Bible: "Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him." We don't know what happened to him. Waiting, and running out of patience.
screen: `FORTY DAYS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WHERE IS HE?` → `UP, MAKE US GODS.`

segments.voice: Aaron doesn't argue. He says, bring me your gold earrings. They pull them off their ears, and he melts them down and shapes a calf. And the people cry out: "These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt." Notice what's strange. Not long before, they heard: no other gods, no carved images. And notice something else. Aaron builds an altar and announces, tomorrow is a feast to the LORD. Some readers think they weren't trying to replace God at all. They wanted a God they could see, one who couldn't go missing on a mountain. The calf was something to hold onto while they waited. Up on the mountain, God tells Moses what's happening, and Moses pleads for the people, reminding God of his promises. And God relents. Then Moses comes down, sees the dancing, and in anger throws the stone tablets to the ground and breaks them at the foot of the mountain. Then comes a very human exchange. Moses asks his brother, what did these people do to you, that you brought such a sin on them? And Aaron says, you know how they are. They gave me the gold. "I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf." As if it just walked out by itself. Christians have often read this chapter as a mirror. In that reading, an idol isn't only a statue. It's whatever people grab hold of when God feels slow, when the answer is late, when the cloud on the mountain says nothing. And the story is honest that even Aaron, the future high priest, made it with his own hands.
screen: `BRING ME YOUR EARRINGS.` · `A GOD THEY COULD SEE.` · `MOSES PLEADS, THEN BREAKS THE TABLETS.` · `THERE CAME OUT THIS CALF.` · then, large: `UP, MAKE US GODS, WHICH SHALL GO BEFORE US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you reach for while waiting. Settle, and breathe. Think about the last time you were waiting for something that mattered: a test result, a reply, a decision, a change that wouldn't come. What did you reach for? Food. The phone. Control. Shopping. A plan B you didn't need yet. Don't scold yourself. Just see it clearly, the way you'd look at a calf someone made out of earrings. Then try waiting here, empty-handed, for the length of the bell. If you pray, you can offer God the waiting itself. The bell holds the time.
Molten calf. The idol cast from the people's melted gold earrings while Moses was still on the mountain.
Your line: impatience makes idols. Today, the next time you're stuck waiting, notice your hand reaching for something, and wait one breath longer before you grab it. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

398.title: Show me your glory (Exodus 33:12–23)
398.hook: Moses in the cleft of the rock sees only God's back as he passes
398.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this passage when talking about knowing God in hindsight, and some spiritual traditions, like the daily examen, look back over the day for where God was present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the molten calf, made of earrings while Moses was late coming down. Your line was impatience makes idols. What did your hand reach for while you waited? Day three hundred ninety-eight.

Have you ever walked into a room just after someone left it? The chair is still warm. A coat still swings on its hook. The air still smells a little like them. You missed them by a minute, but the room still tells you who was here. After the calf, after the broken tablets, Moses has been pleading for his people. And then he asks for something bold. Not for a sign. Not for a plan. In the King James Bible: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory."
screen: `A WARM CHAIR, A SWINGING COAT.` → `AFTER THE CALF, MOSES PLEADS.` → `SHEW ME THY GLORY.`

segments.voice: God says yes, and no. Yes: I will make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll proclaim my name. But no: "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." So God makes a plan, tender and almost playful. There is a place by me, he says, on a rock. I'll put you in a cleft of the rock, and cover you with my hand while I pass by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen." Moses gets to see where God has just been. The glory he asked for is kavod in Hebrew. Lexicons link it to a root meaning heavy, so some readers hear glory as weight: what makes God weighty, real, present. And Moses can only bear it from behind, after it's passed. Readers notice a puzzle here. Just a few verses earlier the same chapter says God spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. So which is it? Some interpreters say the first means closeness, the way friends talk, and the second means the full sight of God, which no one could bear. The text keeps both, side by side. Gregory of Nyssa, a Greek bishop and writer, read it as a picture of following God: you see God's back because you are walking behind him. And the Gospel of John holds both sides too: of Jesus, "we beheld his glory," and a few verses on, "No man hath seen God at any time." Some Christians say faith is often like this: not seeing God's face, but noticing, a little late, that someone was just here.
screen: `YES, AND NO.` · `A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.` · `KAVOD: GLORY THAT HAS WEIGHT.` · `YOU SEE HIS BACK BY FOLLOWING.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT SEE MY BACK PARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for where God has just been. Or, if that language isn't yours, where goodness has just passed. Settle, and breathe. Go back over the last day or two, slowly, like walking back through rooms. Was there a moment that turned out kinder than you expected? A conversation that went right? A worry that quietly didn't happen? A stranger's help? Don't rush to explain it. Just notice the warm chair. If you pray, you can say thank you for what passed by. The bell holds the time.
Kavod. Hebrew for glory, linked to a root meaning heavy: what Moses asked to see, and saw only as God's back, passing by.
Your line: his back, passing by. Tonight, before you sleep, name one place where something good passed through your day, even if you only noticed afterward. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

399.title: Merciful and gracious (Exodus 34:6–7)
399.hook: the name proclaimed: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in steadfast love
399.howItsDone: Some Christians pray with these words from Exodus 34 and Psalm 103, and in Jewish worship the same verses, called the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, are chanted on fast days and the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavod: Moses in the cleft of the rock, seeing only God's back as he passed. Your line was his back, passing by. Where did something good pass through your day? Day three hundred ninety-nine, the end of week fifty-seven.

Early in the morning, Moses climbs Sinai again, carrying two blank stone tablets he has cut himself. The first pair lie broken at the foot of the mountain, smashed after the golden calf. The people have just broken the covenant almost as soon as they made it. If there was ever a moment for God to describe himself as angry, this is it. Moses stands on the mountain. The cloud comes down. And God passes by, and says his own name out loud, and then says what that name means. And it comes right after the calf.
screen: `TWO NEW TABLETS, CUT BY HAND.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE CALF.` → `GOD SAYS WHAT HIS NAME MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin." Merciful, in Hebrew, is rachum. Lexicons link it to the word for a womb, so some readers hear a mother's kind of love in it. Gracious is giving what isn't earned. Longsuffering is a picture in Hebrew: erekh appayim, literally long of nostrils. In Hebrew the nose is where anger shows, and God's takes a long, long time to flare. The Psalms put it plainly: slow to anger. And then the great word: hesed. The King James Bible translates it many ways, mercy, kindness, goodness, lovingkindness, because English doesn't have one word big enough. Hesed is love that keeps its promises. Loyal love, steadfast love, the kind that stays when the other side has given every reason to leave. The passage does go on to say that guilt isn't simply ignored. The text holds mercy and justice together. But look how much weight falls on mercy: kept for thousands. And the Bible keeps coming back to it. Moses quotes it back to God in Numbers. The Psalms sing it: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy." The prophets Joel and Jonah quote it too. What a week: the mountain shook, ten words in two halves, the stranger, the calf, the back of God passing by, and now his name. After the calf, the first thing God says about himself is mercy.
screen: `RACHUM: A MOTHER'S KIND OF LOVE.` · `LONG OF NOSTRILS: SLOW TO ANGER.` · `HESED: LOVE THAT KEEPS PROMISES.` · `ECHOED BY PSALMS AND PROPHETS.` · then, large: `MERCIFUL AND GRACIOUS, LONGSUFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice being slow to anger. Settle, and breathe, and make the breath long, the way the Hebrew pictures a long nose. Think of the person most likely to get under your skin today. Picture the moment it usually happens: the tone, the comment, the thing left undone. Now picture yourself taking one long breath right there, before you answer. Not swallowing what's real. Just slowing it down. Do that twice more, in your mind. If you pray, you can say the words merciful and gracious slowly, as a reminder. The bell holds the time.
Hesed. Hebrew for loyal, steadfast love: love that keeps its promises even after the other side has broken theirs.

Your line: slow to anger. Today, the first time you feel your temper rise, take one long breath before you speak. And that's week fifty-seven: Sinai, lo tirtzach, the stranger, the calf, the cleft, and hesed. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

fork.setup: the people have just broken the covenant with a golden calf. Moses climbs the mountain with new tablets. what's the first thing God says about himself?
options: I am a jealous God.
merciful and gracious, slow to anger.
I will not forgive this people.
fork.reveal: merciful and gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness. mercy comes first, right after the calf.

original.note: Hebrew: steadfast, loyal love. Rendered mercy, kindness or lovingkindness in the King James Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is nice.
what it means: God's own description of his name, given right after the people broke faith: mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love.
what a scholar hears: erekh appayim, long of nostrils, and hesed, covenant loyalty; the formula is echoed in Numbers 14, Psalm 103, Joel 2 and Jonah 4.
